Skeleton, Spine, Skull, and Joints, with the Brain, Nervous, and Endocrine Systems

Unit 1: Anatomy, Positioning, and Medical Language. Lesson 3 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Most plain-film volume is bones, and bone is what drives technique: it is dense, it varies hugely in thickness from a finger to a hip, and it is what the radiographer blames when an image looks flat.

Axial and appendicular

The skeletal system divides in two. The axial skeleton is the center of the body: skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that hang them on: shoulders, arms, hands, pelvis, legs, feet. There are five primary bone types: long bones such as the femur, short bones such as the carpals of the wrist, flat bones such as the ribs, sesamoid bones such as the patella, and irregular bones such as the vertebrae. Marrow inside bone makes blood cells, which is also why bone marrow is one of the most radiosensitive tissues in the body.

The vertebral column

Cervical    7    neck; the atlas and axis at the top carry the skull
Thoracic   12    each pair of ribs attaches here
Lumbar      5    the heavy load-bearing bodies, the thickest part to penetrate
Sacral      5    fused into the sacrum
Coccyx      4 fused bones at the tail
Total      33 bones, so a spine series covers more thickness change than any other exam

Skull and joints

The cranium surrounds the brain: the frontal bone at the forehead, parietal bones at the sides, temporal bones housing the ear structures, the occipital bone at the back, plus the ethmoid and sphenoid inside. The face carries the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, and lacrimal bones. Joints are classified by structure as fibrous, cartilaginous, or synovial, and by function as immovable, slightly movable, or freely movable. The synovial joints, with a capsule and fluid, are the freely movable ones imaging is mostly ordered for.

Brain, nerves, and the endocrine glands

The brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system; the nerves branching from them are the peripheral nervous system. Bone hides soft neural tissue, so plain films show the skull and spine while computed tomography and magnetic resonance show the brain, cord, and discs themselves, which is why a stroke or a disc complaint moves to those rooms. The endocrine glands, at recognition level, are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenals, pancreas, and gonads, and the thyroid is the one imaging and nuclear medicine work with most.

What bone does to technique

  • Density and thickness drive kilovoltage: a hand needs far less than a hip, and a lumbar spine needs a grid where a finger does not.
  • Musculoskeletal pathologies imaging is ordered for are fractures and dislocations, arthritis and joint space loss, bone infection, and tumors.
  • Thin extremities need a small focal spot and short exposures, so detail complaints on extremity work point at focal spot, distance, and motion rather than at dose.
Exam tip: axial is skull, spine, ribs, and sternum; appendicular is the limbs. Count the column 7, 12, 5, 5, and a coccyx. Joints are fibrous, cartilaginous, or synovial. Bone thickness and density pick kilovoltage and decide whether a grid is used.
Remember
The axial skeleton is skull, spine, ribs, and sternum and the appendicular is the limbs and girdles; bones are long, short, flat, sesamoid, or irregular; the column counts 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, and a coccyx; joints are fibrous, cartilaginous, or synovial; the brain, cord, and nerves hide behind bone so cross-sectional rooms image them, and bone thickness decides kilovoltage and whether a grid is needed.
Deeper explanation

Skeleton, Spine, Skull, and Joints, with the Brain, Nervous, and Endocrine Systems, explained slowly

Bone is a technique problem before it is an anatomy problem

A hand and a hip are both bone, and the exposure one needs is nothing like the other. Everything the skeleton does to your equipment follows from two variables: how thick the part is and how dense it is. Thick and dense means more kilovoltage, more exposure, and a grid; thin means a small focal spot, a short exposure, and no grid. That is why a room's technique chart is organized by body part, and why "the extremity images are soft" is a focal spot, distance, and motion question while "the lumbar images are flat" is a grid and kilovoltage question.

The two halves of the skeleton

Axial skeleton          skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum
Appendicular skeleton   shoulders and arms, hands, pelvis, legs, feet
Five bone types         long (femur), short (carpals), flat (ribs),
                        sesamoid (patella), irregular (vertebrae)
Marrow                  inside bone, makes blood cells, and is one of the most
                        radiosensitive tissues there is

That last line is why shielding and collimation matter even on a limb: a field edge that spills onto a pelvis is spilling onto marrow.

The vertebral column, counted and weighted

Region      Count   What it means on the console
Cervical    7       thin neck, low technique, but the shoulders block a lateral
Thoracic    12      ribs and lung behind it, so density changes down the series
Lumbar      5       the thickest part of the spine; grid, higher kilovoltage
Sacral      5 fused heavy, overlapped by bowel gas
Coccyx      4 fused small and low
Total       33      no other single exam crosses this much thickness

A spine series is the best test of whether a room's automatic exposure control and technique chart are honest, because the same patient presents four different thicknesses in one visit.

Skull and joints

The cranium is the frontal bone at the forehead, parietal bones at the sides, temporal bones around the ear structures, the occipital bone at the back, and the ethmoid and sphenoid inside; the face adds mandible, maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, and lacrimal bones. Joints are classified by structure as fibrous (immovable, like skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly movable, like the discs between vertebral bodies), or synovial (freely movable, with a capsule and fluid: knee, shoulder, hip). Synovial joints are what most joint imaging is ordered for, and their service consequence is motion: a freely movable joint has to be supported and imaged quickly.

Soft neural tissue needs a different room

The brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system; the nerves branching out are the peripheral nervous system. Plain films show you the bone around them, so a skull or spine radiograph answers questions about fracture and alignment and nothing about the tissue inside. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance show the brain, cord, and discs directly, which is why stroke, bleed, and disc complaints move to those rooms, and why their table motion, alignment, and reconstruction computers are the service items that matter to neurologic work. The endocrine glands, at recognition level, are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenals, pancreas, and gonads, with the thyroid the one imaging and nuclear medicine work with most.

Musculoskeletal pathology, at recognition level

Fractures and dislocations, degenerative joint disease with narrowed joint spaces, bone infection, and tumors. You do not read them, but you should know that all four are judged on fine detail at the cortex and the joint space, which tells you which image quality factors are clinically load-bearing: focal spot size, object-to-image distance, and motion.

What to memorize

  • Axial is skull, column, ribs, sternum; appendicular is limbs and girdles.
  • Five bone types: long, short, flat, sesamoid, irregular. Marrow is highly radiosensitive.
  • Column 7, 12, 5, 5, and a coccyx, 33 bones in all.
  • Joints fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial. Thickness and density decide kilovoltage and whether a grid is used.
